transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2027-12-06 16:30 UTC
Duration: 54 minutes
Attendees: Jordan Kim (Redwood AE), Priya Nair (Redwood SE), Marco Alvarez (Lyra CTO), Sofia Chen (Lyra Lead ML Eng), Ethan Park (Lyra Infra)

Auto-summary (from Redwood notes): Walkthrough of Redwood Optimize recommendations: batching profiles, prefix/KV prefetch pipeline, cost simulation for Lyra's conversational assistant traffic. Covered TTL, cache hit rate expectations, and pilot plan.

--- Transcript ---
[00:00] Jordan Kim: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, I'm Jordan from Redwood, with Priya our solutions engineer. Uh quick intro, who we've got on the Lyra side?
[00:06] Marco Alvarez: Marco here, CTO. Sofia and Ethan from infra and ML. Thanks for doing this.
[00:10] Sofia Chen: Hey, hi.
[00:12] Priya Nair: Hi all, Priya Nair, SE. We'll run through the Optimize console and then step through a cost sim tailored to the traffic you described. Some notes up front: I'm going to show a couple of prefetch heuristics we often call "lookahead" and a prefix-level KV cache example.
[00:25] Ethan Park: Cool, our big ask is: can we keep p95 under 200 ms and still get cost down vs our current setup? We're mostly on managed endpoints now.
[00:33] Jordan Kim: Good, that aligns. We'll show scenarios where you keep p95 low by using a small batch window plus aggressive KV prefix caching for session contexts.
[00:40] Marco Alvarez: Quick context — we have a multi-tenant assistant, ~120 qps at peak, a lot of short sessions, and long tail of long sessions with context size variance.
[00:50] Priya Nair: Perfect, short sessions are actually where prefix caching gives the best wins. We'll demo two sims: one with sessionization + short TTL and higher prefetch rate, and one with larger TTL but lower prefetch to see the delta in tokens served.
[01:05] Jordan Kim: Also to call out, the cost model will include both per-token inference and egress/extra memory costs from KV; we model cache storage as well as the prefetch overhead.
[01:15] Sofia Chen: When you say prefetch overhead, do you mean additional tokens fetched proactively? That could blow up cost if not tuned.
[01:22] Priya Nair: Exactly — prefetch adds up-front tokens to warm the KV/kv-cache; we simulate hit-rate curves. In our experience a 20-35% prefetch hit improvement often pays for itself for short sessions.
[01:35] Ethan Park: What about concurrency? We plan to run multiple assistants per node. Does locking or session affinity create local hot-spots?
[01:42] Priya Nair: We have options: session affinity to keep KV on same worker or prefix routing to a model variant. Affinity can increase throughput for a given session but reduces bin-packing efficiency. Our console sim shows cost-per-100k-requests under both regimes.
[01:56] Jordan Kim: Okay, let's jump into the console — Priya, can you share your screen?
[02:00] [screen share starts]
[02:05] Priya Nair: I'm in the Optimize tab. Top-left is the batching profile. You can see default batch window is 20ms, concurrency target 48. We'll show adjusting batch window to 10ms and 50ms to see latency vs token cost.
[02:19] Priya Nair: Here is the KV/prefix cache panel — note the prefetch policy, we set a lookahead of 2 tokens for this demo, TTL 30s for prefix entries, and storage size per entry estimate.
[02:30] Marco Alvarez: That TTL seems small — what's the tradeoff?
[02:32] Priya Nair: Short TTL reduces stale context memory and evicts cold sessions faster, cutting cache storage costs, but it increases prefetch frequency for returning sessions. If your session return rate is high, TTL can be longer.
[02:43] Sofia Chen: Our sessions are often 10-30s, so 30s TTL sounds sensible, but we also have periodic long sessions that go 10 minutes.
[02:50] Priya Nair: Right, for long sessions you can enable adaptive TTL where the TTL extends when the session is active more than N minutes, or use a session bucket that pins long sessions to a resident cache.
[03:03] Ethan Park: Show the cost sim then please.
[03:06] Priya Nair: Switching to simulations. I uploaded sample traffic with qps distribution you sent — thank you. First scenario: baseline hosted endpoints, no KV prefetch. p95 is 180 ms, cost per 100k tokens $X (note: placeholder here in the transcript, spreadsheet will have exact).
[03:22] Jordan Kim: (overlapping) And then scenario two enables prefix KV prefetch with a 2-token lookahead and TTL 30s, batch window 15ms, concurrency target 64. That yields a 28% token reduction on average for your short sessions.
[03:36] Marco Alvarez: 28% is huge. Does that assume a cache hit rate of what?
[03:40] Priya Nair: We model hit rate as a function of session length and pattern; here it's about 62% effective hit after prefetch, which includes the lookahead warmups.
[03:50] Sofia Chen: How accurate are these hit rate models for novel prompts? Our assistant generates a lot of dynamic user messages.
[03:56] Priya Nair: Good question — open-domain or highly variable prefixes reduce hit rates. We recommend instrumenting a small pilot to capture real-world prefix similarity. The Console has an "eval-as-cache" sampling mode to estimate similarity.
[04:10] Ethan Park: Any notes on quantization or model variant switching? We run two model sizes in prod.
[04:15] Jordan Kim: Redwood supports model routing; Optimize can recommend a cheaper variant when latency headroom exists. You could route tail requests to the larger model only when needed. That reduces tokens on the big model.
[04:26] Priya Nair: Also mention that some kernels perform better for short sequences — our compile layer picks optimized kernels per sequence length for you, so the cost sim accounts for that.
[04:35] Marco Alvarez: Back to security — our compliance team will want SOC2 and KMS integration. Does prefetch store PII in KV? How do you handle encryption at rest?
[04:44] Jordan Kim: By default Redwood allows encryption at rest using your KMS; you can choose per-tenant key policies. Prefetch entries are treated as transient session context and can be encrypted, logged per your audit policy. We'll share the SOC2 and KMS docs after the call.
[04:58] Sofia Chen: Great. Also, what about logs and audit trails for cache access? We need to see who accessed what.
[05:05] Priya Nair: The Console exposes per-call tracing and audit logs. There's an opt-in KV access log which records reads/writes and can be shipped to your SIEM.
[05:15] Jordan Kim: Let's run a what-if: tighten p95 to 120ms. Priya, run sim?
[05:20] Priya Nair: Running... okay if we cap p95 to 120ms we need batch window 10ms and concurrency 128 across the dedicated pool; that increases cost by ~12% for pure hosted scenario but with prefetch we can recover half of that.
[05:36] Ethan Park: So prefetch helps both cost and p95? Sounds counterintuitive.
[05:40] Priya Nair: It helps latency by avoiding repeated decoding of earlier context and reduces tokens the model needs to generate when much of the context is served from KV. But prefetch itself adds an up-front cost; it's net positive when hit rates are high enough.
[05:53] Marco Alvarez: Any rule of thumb?
[05:55] Priya Nair: For short session distribution like yours: if median session length < 40 tokens and return probability within 30s > 15%, prefetch often pays off.
[06:06] Sofia Chen: Ok how do we measure return probability?
[06:09] Jordan Kim: Instrumentation: sample logs for session IDs and compute inter-arrival times. We can help with a small script — Priya has one in the onboarding kit.
[06:18] [small cross talk] Sofia Chen: (inaudible)
[06:21] Priya Nair: Back to simulations — I'm toggling a policy called "prefetch delta" which limits prefetch to cases where estimated hit probability > 0.4, so we avoid wasted warmups on low-prob prefixes. That reduces wasted tokens in long-tail.
[06:36] Jordan Kim: We've also seen wins by combining batching with prefetch: micro-batches reduce latency penalty while batch-level caching can share prefetched KV across requests in the same window.
[06:47] Ethan Park: That makes sense. Any pitfalls with autoscaling and prefetch surge?
[06:52] Priya Nair: Prefetch spikes can increase short-term token load; we recommend burst capacity or throttles for prefetch during scale-up. Dedicated capacity helps since you can reserve burst headroom.
[07:05] Marco Alvarez: What's the minimum pilot size you recommend to validate this?
[07:08] Priya Nair: 10-15k sessions over 48 hours is usually enough to estimate hit rates and cost impact. We can run a canary on a subset of users.
[07:18] Sofia Chen: We can carve out a 10% user cohort.
[07:21] Jordan Kim: Great. We'll send the cost model spreadsheet with scenario tabs. That will include your traffic, three TTL variants, and prefetch thresholds.
[07:30] Marco Alvarez: Can you also show a dedicated capacity scenario? We care about committed pricing.
[07:34] Priya Nair: Yep switching to dedicated scenario tab. With reserved GPUs and autoscale policies, the cost per 100k tokens drops 18-25% depending on utilization. But commitment and burst options differ.
[07:47] Ethan Park: How do fallbacks work if dedicated capacity is saturated?
[07:50] Jordan Kim: We have smart routing: overflow to hosted compatible variants or smaller model variant. You can set fallbacks per route.
[07:58] Sofia Chen: Anything else on data retention? Our legal team wants KV TTL to be configurable globally and per-team.
[08:04] Priya Nair: Yes, Console supports per-namespace TTLs and retention controls; we can surface a policy screen for your legal team.
[08:13] Marco Alvarez: Alright, I think we're close on next steps. Any objections from Lyra side?
[08:18] Sofia Chen: No objections, just need to validate hit-rate with our actual traffic.
[08:22] Ethan Park: Agree, provisioning sandbox will help.
[08:24] Jordan Kim: Perfect. Recap of next steps: Jordan sends cost model and SOC2/KMS docs; Priya provisions sandbox; Lyra provides traffic CSV and SLOs; schedule pilot kickoff.
[08:36] Marco Alvarez: Sounds good, thanks everyone.
[08:38] Jordan Kim: Thanks all, we'll follow up by EOD with the spreadsheet link.
[08:42] [call ends]
